data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference smuggles induction back in because any decision to act on a theory necessarily assumes its predictive reliability, which is an inductive leap from past survival to future performance.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper can demonstrate a form of 'rational action' that requires zero expectation of future success, the charge of smuggling induction fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference is purely aesthetic or heuristic with no bearing on life-and-death decisions, the pragmatic contradiction dissolves.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Pragmatic inconsistency: While Popper denies the logical validity of induction, the *act* of preferring one theory for practical application (e.g., building a bridge) implicitly assigns it a higher subjective probability or reliability than untested alternatives.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
